blocks.text: Violence is 4–6x more common in the mentally ill than the general population, but mental illness is an attributable risk factor in <==10%== of all crimes; personality disorder, alcohol and drug misuse are all bigger risk factors for violence than mental illness, as are male gender, age 15–30, socioeconomic deprivation and past violence history.

MacArthur study (Monahan & Applebaum 2000): violence in first 20 weeks post-discharge was ==9%== for schizophrenia vs ==19%== depression, ==15%== bipolar, ==17.2%== other psychosis, ==29%== substance misuse, ==25%== personality disorder alone. In the community, ==10%== with schizophrenia committed violence over 12 months vs ==2%== without mental disorder (5x); comorbid substance misuse raised this to ==30%==. Men with schizophrenia are up to 5x more likely convicted of serious violence (Wallace 1998); annual homicide risk with schizophrenia is ~1:3000 (men) and 1:33,000 (women).

Fazel & Danesh (2002): 62 prison surveys, 12 countries, ~22,790 prisoners — psychosis ==3.7%== (men), major depression ==10%==, personality disorder ==65%==; ==1%== of sentenced prisoners have an organic mental disorder.

Shaw (2006): ==34%== of homicides are related to a mental disorder, ==5%== linked to schizophrenia, ==10%== of homicide offenders have active symptoms at the time of offence. Brugha et al. (2005): psychosis is ~10x commoner in prison than the general population.

Penrose's Law (Gunn 2000; Kelly 2007): psychiatric institution occupancy rose inversely with prison occupancy, murder rate and live-birth rate. Related theories: 'prison psychosis' (incarceration as causal agent, disputed) and institutionalisation bias (Seddon 2007, following Foucault — prison as a means of confining undesirable/mentally-ill members of society).

Penrose's Law/hypothesis specifically describes the **INVERSE** relationship between the number of psychiatric beds and the prison population — it is not a direct claim that mental illness causes crime, a subtly different (and wrong) paraphrase often offered as a distractor.

blocks.text: Infanticide Act 1938 (**UK**): mother causes death of her child <12 months by wilful act/omission while the balance of her mind was disturbed by not having fully recovered from birth or from lactation effects. Murder-suicide is defined as suicide of the perpetrator within one week of the homicide; incidence 0.2–0.3/100,000/year. Depression is more common in murder-suicide (20–==60%==) than in homicide alone, while substance misuse/criminal history are less frequent. Classic profiles: a recently-separated depressed middle-aged man with firearm access, or an older male caregiver of an ill/debilitated spouse with new-onset depression and firearm access.

Parricide is rare (==2%== of all homicides); the perpetrator is usually a son aged 12–50 motivated by revenge for sexual abuse or financial gain (Seagrave 2009), typically a spontaneous act during a domestic argument against a background of chronic intrafamilial conflict (Shon & Roberts 2010).

sections.title: 6. Sexual Offending — Epidemiology, Typology & Child Sexual Abuse

blocks.text: Most sex offenders lack a major mental illness (Grubin & Gunn 1991); <==10%== have a mental illness. Sexual offences constitute only ==1%== of all offences (likely an underrepresentation); perpetrators are almost exclusively male, and most have more than one category of deviant sexual behaviour.

Child sexual abuse: ==80%== of offenders against children are a relative (==13%==) or otherwise known to them (==68%==); the offender is usually male (==90%==), 1/3 are adolescents, and up to half of victims are related (girls are twice as likely to be victims). **STEP** project 'high-deviancy' offenders were twice as likely to have prior sexual offences and to have been abused themselves as children. 50–==70%== of paedophiles have another paraphilia; paedophiles are ~2.5x more likely to have physical contact with a child than to be purely voyeuristic/exhibitionistic.

Incest requires penetration by definition; sexual relations with step-relatives are not classified as incest in England (though Scotland includes them). ==30%== of reported incest is against children.

Indecent exposure may relate to exhibitionism or be secondary to alcohol, drugs, or rarely dementia/hypomania; the offender rarely communicates with the victim. Most stop reoffending after conviction; 20–==30%== reoffend, and reoffence-with-conviction carries a poor prognosis (high recidivism). An inhibited, 'guilty' exhibitionist (flaccid) is less risky than an angry, aggressive one (erect while offending).
Most exhibitionism offenders are aged 15–25, not middle-aged as intuition might suggest.

sections.title: 7. Sexual Offending — Reoffending, Predictors & the Abel Study

blocks.text: Abel study (1977–85, n=561 non-incarcerated offenders): ==30%== married, ==40%== had ≥1 year college, ==67%== targeted only females/==12%== only males/==21%== both; ==56%== engaged in non-incestuous behaviour only, ==12%== incestuous only, ==23%== both; boys were molested 5x more often than girls; most had multiple paraphilias, and in >==50%== paraphilic tendencies began before age 18.

75–==80%== of sex offenders have no previous sexual conviction (most convictions are 'first-time'); of those with ≥1 prior conviction, ~==40%== have more than one. Over 6-year follow-up, <==10%== are reconvicted of any sexual offence (rapists ==19%==, **CSA** ==13%== — Hanson et al. 2009), though reconvicted offenders commit very serious crimes; reoffence rate rises with longer observation.

Lowest reconviction risk: index offence against a child within one's own family (incest, <==10%== untreated recidivism). Highest: index offence against a child outside the family — those who molest boys reoffend more (13–==40%==) than those who molest girls (10–==29%==). Rapists are more criminally versatile than child molesters and more likely to reoffend non-sexually than sexually.

Lievore (2004) predictors of sexual reoffending: sexual deviancy/multiple offence types, diverse offending history, offences against boys (higher risk than girls), phallometric response to paedophile or nonsexual-violence stimuli, elevated Hare **PCL-R** score (Rice 1990), reduced self-esteem/impaired victim empathy or increased anger at index offence, own history of childhood sexual abuse, violent sexual fantasies, longstanding social isolation, occupational access to victims, sadomasochistic/paedophilic pornography use, and non-completion of treatment (associated with dissocial traits).
The single best predictor of a **FUTURE** sexual offence is a history of **PREVIOUS** sexual offences — not the severity of the current offence or a specific diagnosis.

blocks.text: Two-type model of schizophrenia-related violence (Steinart 1998): Type 1 — organised delusional systems driving the violence, no prominent childhood conduct-disorder history, diverse offending before diagnosis, may be overrepresented among homicide offenders. Type 2 — disorganised clinical picture, childhood/adult conduct-disorder history, early-onset substance misuse, usually attacks a carer/acquaintance; most schizophrenia-related violence is Type 2.

blocks.text: Threat/control-override (T/C-O) syndrome (Link & Steuve) describes feeling threatened and one's mind being dominated by outside forces. >==50%== of prison inmates misuse substances and >==40%== misuse alcohol (vs ==2%==/==4%== in the general population); acute intoxication is linked with disinhibition/disorganisation and is associated with ~==50%== of non-fatal assaults and ==66%== of murders. Comorbid substance misuse raises the violence risk ratio in schizophrenia from 3.6x to 25x the general population.

Among five discharge diagnoses (depression, bipolar, schizophrenia, mixed **PD**, substance use disorder), substance use disorder carries the **HIGHEST** 6-month violence risk — not schizophrenia. Alcohol/drug problems are more strongly linked to violence than any single mental illness category.

blocks.text: Mood disorders: bipolar disorder's link to violence is unclear, and if present is much lower magnitude (~1/10th) than schizophrenia's. Depression is a risk factor for violence mainly alongside other risk factors (psychosis, substance use) and is a clear risk factor for domestic killings; psychotic depression can produce nihilism leading to 'mercy killings' within a domestic/family setting.

Anxiety disorders occur in 10–==25%== of prisoners with little direct evidence of an offending link, though severe anxiety can cause dissociation/disinhibition. Dissociative/conversion disorders can occur under stress in non-disordered individuals (e.g. soldiers); dissociative/psychogenic amnesia is associated with violence to a known victim where the perpetrator is often aroused or intoxicated — such amnesia is difficult to give clear legal evidence about.

Epilepsy: ~==1%== general population prevalence, 1–==2%== in prison, with no general increase in violent acts; ictal violence is rare and more likely in partial than tonic-clonic seizures. Related concepts referenced in the literature: episodic dyscontrol syndrome (amnesia for explosive violence) and intermittent explosive disorder (**DSM**).

Asperger's syndrome frequently overlaps with schizoid **PD**; some studies show more violent offences/criminal damage than the general population, attributed to theory-of-mind deficits, egocentricity and social-reciprocity deficits — especially relevant to sexual offending, though there is no particular increase in violent sexual offences.

Sleep disorders/parasomnias are commoner in children; when violence occurs in this context it is commoner in males, usually with a prior parasomnia history (including nocturnal enuresis), with sleep deprivation/cannabis/alcohol/caffeine as precursors. The sleepwalking offender usually knows the victim, and appears not to hear cries or recognise the victim during the episode.

blocks.text: Malingering is intentional feigning of symptoms for a specific gain; assessment tools include **SIRS**, **SIMS** (structured inventories of reported/malingered symptoms) and the **TOMM** (test of malingered memory); polygraphs are used in the **US** but rarely the **UK**.

Munchausen syndrome is a factitious illness with intentionally created symptoms to assume the sick role without external incentive (specified as psychological or physical); Munchausen-by-proxy is factitious illness induced in a child/dependent. Associated with personality disorder, attention-seeking, masochistic and medication-seeking behaviours; management involves safeguarding, treating any depression, and limiting behaviours (e.g. a hospital register).

Morbid jealousy (Othello syndrome) has a core belief of the partner's infidelity, commonest with paranoid **PD** or an underlying psychotic condition, often with confirmatory behaviours (stalking, repeated calls); significant risks include partner/child harm, self-harm, substance misuse, domestic violence and homicide.

Erotomania (De Clerambault's syndrome) is commoner in females — the belief that someone (often more successful) is in love with them, associated with psychotic disorders; Mullen (2008) links it to stalking or evolving pathological jealousy, with violence occurring on rejection of the perpetrator.

Ganser syndrome is a hysterical dissociative disorder featuring approximate answers, clouding of consciousness with disorientation, psychogenic physical symptoms (analgesia/hyperaesthesia) and pseudohallucinations (not all features always present); patients are amnesic for the abnormal behaviour. It is often seen in prisoners, especially military prisoners and those absenting themselves from the army/navy.

sections.title: 15. Special Offender Groups — Women, Young Offenders, Ethnic Minorities & Deaf Offenders

blocks.text: Only ==1 in 5== offenders is a woman (male:female conviction ratio ~5:1); women's peak offending age is 2–3 years earlier than men's (14 vs 17–18). Women's index offence is more often 'romantic'/domestic; ==68%== of imprisoned women are there for non-violent offences (vs ==47%== of men); women steal fewer/lower-value items and receive more psychiatric pleas and disposals than men.

Women in custody are 5x more likely to have mental health problems than women in the general population; up to ==80%== have diagnosable mental health problems, and ==1 in 5== remand women (2003) had psychosis. **HMIP** (2006/07): ==19%== of women had attempted suicide in the year before custody (~3x the male rate); ==33%== had an accommodation need; ==31%== had an alcohol misuse problem (vs ==42%== of men); ==60%== had emotional wellbeing problems recorded (vs ==36%== of men).

Age of criminal responsibility: 10 (England & Wales), 8 (Scotland). Juvenile offenders are 10–17, young offenders 18–21, adult offenders ≥21, handled via the youth offending service. Placement options: Young Offender Institutes (18–21, and 15–17 for juveniles), secure training centres/detention schools (up to 17), secure children's homes (12–16), adolescent secure hospitals.

Ethnic minority groups make up ==15%== of the **UK** population but are overrepresented in prison and secure settings, with documented concerns about more schizophrenia diagnoses, more involuntary admission, more seclusion/restraint, and more custodial sentences among **BME** patients.

Deaf offenders have a higher prevalence of mental disorder and face communication-related barriers to services; the **UK** has three general psychiatric hospitals, one high-secure deaf service and several independent hospitals providing inpatient care. Deafness may affect an individual's fitness to plead.

sections.title: 16. Victims of Crime & Patients as Victims

blocks.text: Crime victimisation impairs occupational, parenting, relationship and general social functioning; non-violent crime has relatively little impact on life satisfaction, but the more violent the crime, the greater the social dysfunction. Sexual assault victims are particularly prone to social withdrawal (Golding et al. 2002); >==50%== report a continuously restricted social life even 15–30 months after the assault.

**PTSD** is more frequent in the forensic population; there is no definite causal link between offending and **PTSD** in perpetrators, but both perpetrators and victims carry high **PTSD** risk (higher in victims) — ~==20%== of prisoners have diagnosable **PTSD**. Complex **PTSD** is associated with prolonged childhood abuse with common comorbid substance misuse; psychosis combined with **PTSD** can increase positive symptoms and paranoid/violent thoughts. The index offence itself can be a significant traumatic trigger for forensic inpatients in up to ==70%== of cases, especially if unplanned, the offender was disinhibited, and there was no prior forensic history.

Khalifeh et al. (2015), National Crime Survey: ==40%== of patients with severe mental illness were victims of crime in the past year vs ==14%== of the general population (**OR** 2.8); for violent assault specifically, ==19%== of patients vs ==3%== of controls (**OR** 5.3). Women with severe mental illness were 4x more likely to be victims of domestic violence, 4x more likely victims of sexual violence, and 10x more likely to be victims of any community violence.

blocks.text: Courts can remand to hospital under Section 35 for assessment (up to 28 days initially, maximum 12 weeks) to produce a report on mental disorder, or under the rarely-used Section 36 for treatment (28 days, renewable to 12 weeks total — only 16 recorded uses in England & Wales to March 2007). If the Crown Court finds the accused unfit to plead, a 'trial of facts' follows.

Disposals after a full trial or trial of facts: absolute discharge (acquittal), probation/health supervision order (conditional discharge), prison, or hospital disposal (with restriction/supervision/guardianship orders available in some cases). Section 37 guardianship orders are little used (supervision orders being more available); they last 6 months initially, renewable by the Responsible Clinician (**RC**) at 6 months then yearly, and empower the guardian to require residence, attendance for treatment/education, and access.

Disposal outcome tracks diagnosis, not just offence severity: among homicide perpetrators with a personality disorder as the primary diagnosis, ==92%== are imprisoned and only ~==4%== receive a hospital disposal — almost the mirror image of schizophrenia-primary perpetrators (==29%== imprisoned, ==71%== hospital order). A classic cross-cutting legal/clinical trap.

sections.title: 18. Secure Settings, Care Models & Multi-Agency Working

blocks.text: High secure units hold MDOs of grave/immediate risk; medium secure units serve high-risk MDOs; low secure units hold MDOs with limited violence/absconding risk. Young Offender Institutes, detention schools (higher relational security than YOIs), secure children's homes (lower security) and adolescent secure hospitals (medium secure) exist for younger offenders.

Community care models: Parallel Care (inpatient medium secure care and community care run in parallel with the same service), Integrated Care (general psychiatric services take over long-term rehabilitation and lower-security readmissions post-discharge), and Hybrid Care (integrated model plus a period of 'shared care' post-discharge, with forensic services retaining long-term care for a subset of high-risk offenders).

~==70%== of supervised offenders in England & Wales are on probation on discharge from secure institutions. Probation officer roles: pre-sentence assessment, monitoring sentenced offenders, advising the parole board, supervising licence/recall, supervising/reporting breach of community sentences, advising on local resources, and directly providing psychological-programme support.

Prison inreach teams (now in ~==87%== of **UK** prisons) link to primary care. **NOMS** joins up prison and probation services and advises government on policy. **MAPPA** (Multi-Agency Public Protection Arrangements) covers MDOs convicted of a specified sexual/violent offence sentenced >12 months, or hospital-detained/conditionally discharged, providing an interagency framework for managing violent and sexual offenders.

Three security domains: physical (fences/locks, soft cutlery, removal of sharps/hanging points), relational (training, communication, meaningful activities — its absence undermines physical security), procedural (searches, incident learning, staff vetting, governance). Observation levels: general (location known, not in eyesight), intermittent, within eyesight (high/imminent risk), and within arm's length (highest risk of rapid self-harm, e.g. swallowing an object).

Section 17 leave decisions weigh mental state stability, insight, staff rapport, treatment engagement, and past leave behaviour; leave forms specify purpose/conditions, destination, escort availability and transport — this is distinct from parole.

sections.title: 20. Violence Risk Assessment — Concepts, Approaches & Stages

blocks.text: The Butler Committee defined dangerousness as 'a propensity to cause serious physical injury or lasting psychological harm' — a term now replaced by risk assessment/management. The Ritchie report (Christopher Clunis's killing of Jonathan Zito) identified failures of individual-practitioner risk assessment and management.

Prediction problems: low base rate (serious violence measured at <==1%== even in the severely mentally ill — Wallace 1998) severely limits predictive value and raises false positives; risk is multifactorial, changes over time, and factor interactions are often unknown. Risk factors are static (fixed/historical, e.g. family history of suicide), stable (enduring but somewhat modifiable, e.g. **PD** diagnosis) or dynamic (fluctuating, e.g. acute anxiety/akathisia) — dynamic factors can multiply the effect of underlying static/stable factors if unaddressed.

blocks.title: Static, stable and dynamic risk factors

blocks.text: Homicide inquiries have identified recurring problems: failure to consider carers' views, undue emphasis on patients' civil liberties, failure to properly implement the **MHA**, taking a cross-sectional rather than longitudinal view of risk, and failure to share information.

Three approaches: clinical (subjective/intuitive, poor predictive value — only ~1/3 of pure clinical judgments estimated correct retrospectively), actuarial (algorithmic numerical probability, superior for predicting violence/sexual reoffending but insensitive to change, high false-positive rate, poor cross-setting generalisation, over-weights static/stable factors), and structured professional judgment (combines evidence-based risk factors with individual clinical assessment, e.g. **HCR-20**). Neither actuarial nor structured judgment should replace conventional clinical assessment.

Bouch & Marshall's risk-assessment stages: (A) identify need for a full structured assessment, (B) assess static/stable/dynamic/future factors and protective factors, (C) formulate risk in the current context, (D) consider interventions/support level, (E) anticipate intervention impact, (F) develop a management plan with short/long-term actions, (G) review and revise as risk factors change.

sections.title: 22. Fitness to Plead & the R v Pritchard Criteria

blocks.text: Fitness to plead concerns mental ability to comply with trial proceedings; physical conditions (deafness/muteness) are also relevant. There is a presumption of fitness; the factors are relevant only at time of trial (not arrest/charging), and amnesia for the offence does not itself interfere with fitness to plead.

R v Pritchard criteria — a defendant is unfit to plead if incapable of: understanding the charge(s); deciding whether to plead guilty; exercising the right to challenge jurors; instructing solicitors/counsel; following the course of proceedings; giving evidence in their own defence.

sections.title: 23. McNaughten Rules, Diminished Responsibility & Capacity to Form Intent

blocks.text: McNaughten Rules (1843), 4 components: a defect of reason (impaired, not mere failure to exercise it); due to a disease of the mind (not externally caused); leading to loss of appreciation of the nature/quality of the act; such that the accused did not realise the act was wrong (legally or morally). Burden of proof lies with the defence; the jury decides; disposals remain flexible (not automatically hospital confinement).

Diminished responsibility reduces a murder charge to manslaughter; the defence must show absence of mens rea (act remains unlawful, but no malice aforethought). Disposal for murder is restricted, but flexible for manslaughter; females and those with no criminal record are more likely to have this defence granted.

Capacity to form intent: symptoms that can prevent formation of the relevant mental processes include specific relevant delusions, an abnormal mood state (severe depression/mania) with psychomotor change or impaired concentration, and severe cognitive impairment (dementia/chronic schizophrenia) — this excludes voluntary intoxication (doctrine of prior fault, as a person is expected to foresee this). If diminished capacity is upheld, acquittal or conviction for a lesser offence may follow.

Legal-terminology precision is heavily tested: actus reus = the (voluntary) physical act; mens rea = intent; doli incapax = incapable of crime (below age of criminal responsibility); habeas corpus = right to a hearing on the legality of detention; corpus delicti = the factual evidence/body of the offence. These near-synonymous Latin terms are deliberately confused as both single-best-answer and **EMI** matching items.

blocks.text: Automatism is a plea that the defendant's actions were not under conscious control (unwilled, involuntary bodily movements), negating the actus reus. It is a rare plea. Sane automatism (automatism simpliciter, extrinsic/one-off cause) leads to complete acquittal; insane automatism (intrinsic cause, likely to recur) leads to a not-guilty-by-reason-of-insanity type disposal. Courts limit the defence where the defendant exercised some control, the condition falls under insanity rules, or there was prior fault.

R v Burgess (1991) held somnambulism could be genetic/internal and thus classified as sane or insane at the judge's discretion.

blocks.text: Culpable homicide lies between manslaughter and murder: involuntary (unintended death from assault or negligence) or voluntary (intentional/reckless act mitigated by provocation or diminished responsibility).

Intoxication is rarely used as a defence. Involuntary intoxication (a spiked drink, a prescribed medication's effect, reckless use of a non-dangerous substance, or an irresistible dependence-driven impulse) is a valid defence/mitigating factor; voluntary self-induced intoxication is not a defence.

Voluntary intoxication can **NEVER** found an insanity plea or defence to a basic-intent crime (e.g. sexual assault) — even when it directly precipitated the offence. Contrast with involuntary intoxication (spiked drink, prescribed medication, reckless use of a non-dangerous substance, dependence-driven irresistible impulse), which **IS** a valid defence/mitigating factor.

sections.title: 25. Mitigating Factors & Amnesia for the Offence

blocks.text: Mitigating factors reducing culpability: provocation, age/vulnerability, mental disorder or **LD**, involuntary intoxication, remorse, and a limited role in the offence.

Kopelman (2002): amnesia is commonly claimed in violent offences, especially homicide (25–==45%== of occasions); other associated conditions include psychosis, epilepsy, hysterical personality traits, parasomnias, organic brain disorder, hypoglycaemia and head injury. Amnesia itself has no legal implication in England & Wales absent automatism, and does not render someone unfit to plead — though credibility issues can arise without expert-witness support, particularly for fitness to plead/to be interviewed and reliability of an amnesic syndrome.

sections.title: 26. The Psychiatrist's Role — Evidence, Reports, Expert Witnesses & Human Rights

blocks.text: The case-law test for fitness to give evidence: understanding the question, applying one's mind to answering it, and conveying answers intelligibly to the jury. Three types of false confession are recognised: voluntary, coerced-compliant, coerced-internalised — influenced by situational factors (custody/isolation/interrogation) and individual factors (mental disorder, incapacity); assessment involves reviewing transcripts and vulnerability/cognitive/intelligence/disorder factors.

Key psychiatric roles in the criminal justice pathway: assessing suspects in custody, advising on mental-health diversion and medical needs, advising on fitness to be interviewed and need for an appropriate adult, advising on fitness to plead/stand trial, arranging remand-to-hospital transfer, and advising on sentencing options.

**GMC** good-practice principles for reports (2006, paras 63, 65–67): be honest and trustworthy; ensure documents are not false or misleading, taking reasonable steps to verify information and not deliberately omitting relevant information; act without unreasonable delay; be honest in all spoken/written evidence and make clear the limits of one's knowledge/competence.

Three witness types: ordinary (witness to fact, not opinion), professional (comments on clinical state with some prior involvement), expert (writes reports/statements on mental disorder or a specific issue) — expert witnesses provide advisory, actuarial, clinical or experimental expertise.

**ECHR** articles most relevant to forensic practice: Article 2 (right to life — the state has a positive duty to safeguard prisoners/those in custody), Article 3 (prohibition of torture/degrading treatment), Article 5 (right to personal liberty — authorises detention of persons of 'unsound mind'; underpins the deprivation of liberty safeguards), Article 8 (right to private and family life, widely interpreted).
